note_on_f1: F1 is intentionally omitted from this comparison. In the notebook's original cached run, the static/combined-rule baselines' F1 was computed at each method's own best decision threshold (via precision_recall_curve), while the LSTM/RF/Logistic-Regression F1 was computed at a fixed 0.5 threshold -- an unfair, apples-to-oranges comparison that artificially shrinks (or could even reverse) the apparent ML advantage. AUC and PR-AUC (average precision) are threshold-independent and were computed identically for every method, so they are reported here instead. Recomputing a fair F1 would require rerunning inference with the saved models (kept only in the team's Colab/Drive session, not in this repo) at one consistent threshold for every method -- flagged as a future to-do, not done here.

standalone_per_feature_auc.note: Single-feature AUC (last timestep only) against each attack type in isolation -- used to sanity-check that no feature is suspiciously perfect (would indicate a data leak) and that each feature specializes physically-sensibly.

no_leakage_check: No feature reaches a suspiciously perfect AUC (max observed is 0.99 for qber vs IR, which is expected since IR is designed to be QBER-loud). Every feature specializes in exactly the attack type decoy-state theory predicts: sifted_rate and y1_lower catch PNS but not IR; qber-family features catch IR but not PNS. This rules out label leakage or circular feature construction.
corrected_headline_finding: The QBER-only static threshold (today's real-world status quo) is genuinely broken on PNS (PR-AUC 0.17, barely above random). However, a single additional engineered feature (sifted/throughput rate) closes most of that gap even with a plain no-ML combined rule (PR-AUC 0.80). The LSTM's improvement on top of good feature engineering is real and consistent across all 7 seeds but modest (~0.85-0.89 PR-AUC on PNS vs 0.78-0.80 for the combined rule / Random Forest) -- roughly a 5-9 point PR-AUC gain, not a dramatic rescue. This is a more defensible and more interesting claim than 'ML beats static thresholds': feature engineering informed by decoy-state theory closes most of the gap, and sequence modeling adds a smaller but consistent further improvement, while also providing a single unified detector without hand-picked per-attack-type rules.
